name: Ghana
summary: There is no forced heirship: a will can dispose of the estate, but the court can interfere where reasonable provision is not made for a child under 18 (Wills Act 1971, s. 13). Without a will, the Intestate Succession Law of 1985 shares the estate among spouse, children and others. Trusts are recognised; no private foundation law was found.
family_claims: Wills Act 1971 (Act 360) s. 13: court may interfere where no reasonable provision for a child under 18. Intestacy is governed by PNDCL 111 of 1985 (uniform rules for spouse and children).
foreign_law_note: No source found on foreign law for resident foreigners' estates.
trust_note: Trusts are recognised in common law and equity; statutes named are the Trustees (Incorporation) Act 1962 (Act 106) and the Public Trustee Ordinance 1952, with land held in trust needing registration. Charitable trusts are recognised. No private-foundation law was found.
open_questions: Whether the Wills Act gives adults or spouses any claim was not sourced.
Foundation law and Ghana's treatment of foreign trusts not found.
Customary-law estates are outside these rules in some cases; not sourced.

Hague Trusts Convention: The HCCH status table (checked 2026-10-16) lists 14 Contracting Parties; this country is not one of them and no UK, Dutch or Chinese extension covers it, so the 1985 Convention is not in force here.

sources.title: Intestate succession in Ghana: how PNDCL 111 shapes families after death
